# No universal equal-volume level trimming with a singleton centroid graph

The equal-volume centroid-graph theorem does NOT extend by universally
trimming the fibers to equal-volume levels. The failure below holds for
ANY choice of trimmed subbodies at a single level, not just homothetic
trimming. All fibers are positive dimensional, and every index is
strictly active at the chosen level. Nestedness across levels cannot
repair the obstruction at that one level.

This is an auxiliary-construction counterexample, not a counterexample
to OC. Indeed an actual middle-fiber centroid of the same body has a
strictly stronger depth guarantee than its OC threshold.

## 1. An exact rational convex body with nine fibers

Let n=2,d=1. Over the four corner indices of [0,2]^2, prescribe the
unit intervals

    K_(0,0)=K_(2,2)=[1/2,3/2],
    K_(2,0)=K_(0,2)=[-3/2,-1/2].                    (1)

Let C be their lifted convex hull in R^2 x R. It is compact and convex,
and its projection is [0,2]^2. It has nonempty three-dimensional
interior: the four lifted interval centers

    (0,0,1),(2,0,-1),(0,2,-1),(2,2,1)

have affine-difference determinant 16. Thus C is an actual convex
body in the task's ambient space, with the standard lattice Z^2 x R.

Its exact integer fibers are the four in (1), the four edge-midpoint
fibers

    K_(1,0)=K_(0,1)=K_(2,1)=K_(1,2)=[-1/2,1/2],

and the central fiber

    K_(1,1)=[-3/2,3/2].                              (2)

For a direct check of all sections, write a=z_1/2,b=z_2/2. A convex
representation of the base using the four corners has weights

    lambda_11=s, lambda_10=a-s, lambda_01=b-s,
    lambda_00=1-a-b+s,
    max(0,a+b-1)<=s<=min(a,b).

The corresponding center height is 1-2a-2b+4s. The original interval
offsets add exactly [-1/2,1/2], independently of those weights. Thus
this formula gives the whole fiber and verifies (1)--(2) at every
integer point of the square. There are no other integer base points.

All eight boundary fibers have length one, and the central fiber has
length three. Hence q=1 and M=H_1(S)=11.

## 2. No choice of level subbodies has the required centroid graph

Fix ANY 0<t<1, for example the rational level t=3/4. Every original
fiber has length STRICTLY greater than t, so all nine indices belong
to the active level under either the convention w_z>=t or w_z>t.
Suppose one chooses convex subbodies

    K_z(t) subset K_z, |K_z(t)|=min(|K_z|,t)=t

at every index, with centroids c_z(t). In dimension one they are
closed intervals of length t. At the two high corners their centroids
satisfy

    c_(0,0),c_(2,2)>=1/2+t/2,

whereas at the two low corners

    c_(2,0),c_(0,2)<=-1/2-t/2.

Let T_t be their finite lifted centroid graph and G_t=conv(T_t).
The average of the two high-corner centroid points and the average
of the two low-corner centroid points both have the SAME integer base
(1,1), but their continuous coordinates obey

    x_high>=1/2+t/2,
    x_low<=-1/2-t/2.

These are distinct. Both belong to (G_t)_(1,1), and their segment
does too. Thus

    G_t intersect (Z^2 x R) != T_t.                  (3)

The selected central centroid is just one point and cannot make the
two different forced averages coincide. The choices at the other
five indices do not affect this contradiction.

In fact ANY selection of one point in each original corner interval
already has distinct high- and low-diagonal averages. The argument
therefore persists if the proposed construction uses other centroids,
dominated submeasures, or arbitrary selectors supported in the same
corner fibers. The volume-t estimates above give an explicit positive
separation, rather than relying on equality at a support endpoint.

This refutes the universal single-level construction. In particular,
there cannot be a family for all t that also satisfies nestedness and
the claimed centroid-graph property at each active level.

## 3. Convex compatibility itself requires extra central volume

There is an even more direct volume obstruction. The Minkowski average
of the two selected high-corner intervals has length t and center at
least 1/2+t/2. Its upper endpoint is therefore at least 1/2+t. The
average of the two selected low-corner intervals has lower endpoint
at most -1/2-t. Any convex set containing these four lifted trimmed
intervals must contain both averages and the segment between their
extreme endpoints in its central integer fiber. That fiber must have
length at least

    1+2t>t.                                         (4)

Thus no convex body can induce precisely these four length-t corner
subintervals together with a central interval of length t. This proves
failure of convex compatibility before any Helly or layer integration
step. The lower bound 1+2t is attained for the corner intervals chosen
as close to zero as allowed: [1/2,1/2+t] on the high corners and
[-1/2-t,-1/2] on the low corners.

## 4. The natural nested homothetic trimming fails explicitly

The usual centroid-based choice is

    K_z^hom(t)=g_z+(t/|K_z|)(K_z-g_z), 0<t<1.

These intervals are nested in t and all have length t. They have
centers +1 at the high corners, -1 at the low corners, and 0 at all
other indices. In particular the central trimmed interval is
[-t/2,t/2]. The high-corner Minkowski average is

    [1-t/2,1+t/2],

which lies strictly above the central trimmed interval for t<1.
The low-corner average lies strictly below it. Convexifying all these
homothetic trims forces central length at least 2+t, not t.
Their centroid graph has at its central integer section at least
the whole interval [-1,1]. Thus this natural choice fails both
convex compatibility and the singleton centroid-graph requirement,
despite having exact prescribed volumes and perfect nestedness.

## 5. What an extra radius variable can and cannot fix here

If a proposed convex lift uses an extra real radius coordinate and
requires its fixed-radius section to induce exactly the selected
volume-t subbodies, that section is itself convex. Equation (4) rules
out such a lift on this example: its central section necessarily
acquires extra volume. An equality of the form |K_z(t)|=min(w_z,t)
cannot then be retained at all integer fibers.

This does not rule out a different lift which changes the level
measure, allows extra central volume, uses nonhorizontal level cuts,
or abandons singleton centroid graphs. Such a construction would need
an additional proved measure/depth identity; the present example does
not supply or presume one.

## 6. The body itself satisfies the desired depth bound

Take y=(1,1,0), the actual centroid of the central interval in (2).
Every closed ambient halfspace containing y captures length at least
3/2 from that interval alone: a nonconstant restriction is a closed
halfline containing its midpoint, while a constant restriction
contains the whole interval. Consequently

    depth_S(y)>= (3/2)/11=3/22>1/8=gamma_1/2^2.

All other fiber contributions are nonnegative. Thus the obstruction
is to the proposed equal-volume level construction, with all lattice
and intrinsic measures unchanged, and not to the original conjecture.
